analytic.title: Scheduling Analysis of Real-Time Systems with Precise Modeling of Cache Related Preemption Delay

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Accurate timing analysis is key to efficient embedded system synthesis and integration. Caches are needed to increase the processor performance but they are hard to use because of their complex behaviour especially in preemptive scheduling. Current approaches use simplified assumptions or propose exponentially complex scheduling analysis algorithms to bound the cache related preemption delay at a context switch. We present an conservative polynomial algorithm that extends real-time scheduling analysis to consider cache effects due to the preempted and the preempting task for the preemption delay. Dataflow analysis on task level is combined with real-time scheduling analysis to determine the response time including cache related preemption delay for each task accurately. The experiments show significant improvement in analysis precision over previous polynomial approaches for typical embedded benchmarks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Caches are needed to increase processor performance but they are hard to use in real-time systems because of their complex behaviour. While it is difficult enough to determine cache behaviour for a single task, it becomes even more complicated if preemptive task scheduling is included. Preemptive task scheduling means that task execution can be interrupted by higher priority tasks. In this case, cache improvements can be strongly degraded by frequent replacements of cache blocks.

There are several approaches to make caches more predictable and efficient. One approach is to partition the cache sets and to reserve these partitions for individual tasks [11]. The advantage is that cache lines do not have to be reloaded after interrupts and between consecutive executions of the same task. Also, cache behaviour becomes (partly) orthog-onal for tasks and therefore more predictable. Task layout techniques are suggested in [5] which aim at minimising the inter-task interference in the instruction cache. Another approach is to lock frequently used cache blocks. Such techniques have been investigated by [9] [4] [15]. These approaches come at an area and power cost as they require greater caches and background memory to become effective. Therefore, heterogeneous memory architectures with caches and scratch-pad SRAM have been introduced [7], where the scratch-pad can hold frequently used cache blocks. Compiler techniques for such architectures have been proposed by [13].

While cache partition and lock strategies are certainly a very useful add-on to improve cache predictability and efficiency, they do not solve the general cache behaviour problem which is critical for larger systems of tasks. Simplified approaches extend the known response time analysis with fixed context switch costs [3], while more recent approaches [10] [12] use data flow analysis to determine the maximum cache related preemption delay (CRPD). Such CRPD estimation has been integrated in scheduling analysis [14] and [10]. These approaches assume a single delay for each preemption, which might lead to pessimistic overestimation [16].

In this paper, we integrate cache related preemption calculation into scheduling analysis. The proposed algorithms are polynomial and consider the cache effects of previous conservative polynomial approaches [14] [3]. Additionally, it also covers some cache effects as described in the exponential scheduling analysis by [10]. The proposed approach supports hard real-time system analysis but can also be useful for rapid design space exploration.

This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the background and reviews related work on CRPD analysis. Section 3 presents three approaches that compute the preemption costs and that bound the total number of preemptions accurately. The experiments in Section 5 show significant improvement in analysis precision over previous polynomial approaches. Finally, we conclude in Section 6.

div.head: Preemptive scheduling analysis
div.p: The scheduling method presented in this paper is based on response time analysis (RTA) [3] [2] [8]. The computational model assumes a fixed priority periodic task sets with deadline at the end of a period.

The worst case response time occurs when all tasks are released at the same time point (critical instant). An iterative approach is used to calculate the response time of a given task. The approach tries to allocate in a time window w the task τ i 's computation time C i , the tasks blocking time B i and the interference produced by the execution of higher priority tasks. The blocking time is the maximum time that the task can be delayed by lower priority tasks due to resource contention. The process is finished when the window stops growing (w n+1 i = w n i ). If the resulted response time for any task is greater than its deadline (w
div.formula: n+1 i = w n i = R i > D i
div.p: ), the task-set is not schedulable. The iterative relation is shown below:
div.formula: w n+1 i = C i + B i + ∑ j∈hp(i) w n i T j •C j (1)
div.p: The term hp(i) denotes the set of tasks with a higher priority than task τ i . Task τ 1 has the highest and τ n the lowest priority.

div.head: Accounting for cache interference
div.p: In an embedded system with cache the context switch time depends on the contents of the cache. When a task τ j preempts τ i some cache blocks are removed by τ j and have to be reloaded by τ i after it resumes. Five possible ways to determine the CRPD are given in [3]: 1.) The time to refill the entire cache. 2.) The time to refill the cache blocks displaced by the preempting task. 3.) The time to refill the cache blocks used by the preempted task. 4.) The time to refill the maximum number of useful cache blocks that the preempted task may hold in the cache when a preemption occurs. Useful blocks are those that are likely to be used again [6]. 5.) The time to refill the intersection of blocks between the preempting and preempted task [10].

The approach in [3] considers the penalty according to number 1 and 2 of this list. The following equation is used for the response time analysis. It differs from Equation 1only by an additional γ i which corresponds to the additional preemption delay due to the cache interference caused by the preempting task τ j :
div.formula: w n+1 i = C i + B i + ∑ j∈hp(i) w n i T j • (C j + γ j )(2)
div.p: Petters presents in [14] an approach that considers the preempted task only. The response time of a task is computed by
div.formula: R i = C i + B i + ∑ j∈hp(i) (E j (R i ) •C j + ∆ j,i (R i ))(3)
div.p: where E j (R i ) denotes the worst case number of releases of task τ j within the interval R i . For fixed priority preemptive scheduling this number is given by E j (R i ) = R i T j . In the following we use the term E j (R i ) to allow more general scheduling policies, such as interrupts. The preemption delay ∆ j,i (R i ) which task τ j imposes on lower priority tasks is computed by an iterative approach. The number of preemptions is bounded by E j (R i ).

Approaches such as [10] [12] have been proposed to reduce such overestimation by considering the preempting and preempted task. With a data flow analysis the maximum number of useful cache blocks of the preempted task and the maximum number of used cache blocks of the preempting task are computed. In [10] the response time of tasks for fixed priority preemptive scheduling is computed by constructing an integer linear programming problem. Exponential number of equations are set up to describe the system, making it difficult for industrial use. Their solution is not exact because best case execution times are assumed, which are known to be hard to compute and every preemption costs the same time delay.

Current approaches for real time scheduling analysis with CRPD either propose an exponential scheduling analysis considering the preempted and the preempting task [10] or propose polynomial time algoriths which consider preempted task [14] or preempting task [3] only.

div.head: Real-time scheduling analysis
div.p: An accurate determination of CRPD is known to be very complex. Several approximations, polynomial and exponential ones, have been proposed. As complexity in architecture grows scheduling analysis techniques cannot afford to grow equally complex. Certainly they would lead to more precise results, but these algorithms would not be applicable to real-life problems. This is our motivation to develop an as accurate algorithm as possible which has at most polynomial time complexity.

The problem separates into three parts. The first is the computation of the preemption delay of two tasks. We use the methodology of [16] which is briefly explained in 3.1. The second part is the computation of the number n of preemptions. The third part is to find the n highest preemptions costs. We propose three algorithms to solve the last two parts.

A simple approximation which considers that all preemption costs take place, is described in Section 3.2. This is shown in Fig. 1. However note, that task τ 2 actually blocks the second and third preemption on τ 3 . A polynomial-time algorithm is proposed in Section 3.3 which takes indirect preemptions into account. Finally we take a closer look on infeasible preemption costs in Section 4.

div.head: Preemption cost calculation
div.p: The objective is to find the maximum CRPD, when task τ j preempts τ i . A task is represented by its control flow graph (CFG). In previous work [16] the preempted and preempting task are considered for CRPD calculation. The preempted task can only reload cache blocks that are accessed again after the preemption. The maximum number of so-called useful cache blocks is computed by two iterative data flow analysis algorithms. First, to compute the set of cache blocks that are available (reaching cache blocks) at each node in the CFG, and secondly to compute the set of cache blocks that are potentially reused (live cache blocks) at each node. The intersection of both sets is the set of useful cache blocks.

The set of used cache blocks of the preempting task is a second upper bound of potentially replaced cache blocks. This property is computed also with an iterative data flow analysis. The set of reaching cache blocks at the last node of the CFG determines the total number of used cache blocks. Finally the intersection of the used cache blocks (at the last node) of the preempting task and useful cache blocks at node n k of the preempted task determines the CRPD at a node n k . The maximum is denoted by δ j,i .

For multiple preemptions we refined the analysis, by computing the nth preemption cost, assuming that the worst case n -1 preemptions have taken place. Because the maximum number of useful cache blocks are found within loops, the analysis gain was marginal while it required potentially exponential time complexity. For this paper, we duplicated the maximum CRPD within a loop by the number of loop iterations and ordered all CRPD costs in descending order (without removing duplicates). This allows us an graduation of preemption costs for first, second, •••, nth preemption cost, denoted as δ n j,i , with polynomial time complexity. A second simplification concerns the set of used cache blocks. In [16] we used a state-based approach, where several sets of used cache blocks are considered. The proposed scheduling analysis requires each preemption delay to consider all cache states (of the preempting task). The reason is further explained in 3.3. We fulfill this condition by taking the union of all used cache blocks at the last node of the preempting task. These two simplifications were the sacrifices to a polynomial time scheduling algorithm.

div.head: Indirect preemptions
div.p: The drawback of the summation model of Equation 6is that every preemption is assumed to take place. However, preemptions that are masked by some intermediate tasks cannot remove any additional cache blocks. Fig. 2 shows the response times of four tasks. A preemption delay is denoted by the patterned area. Note, that the first preemption of τ 1 affects τ 2 , τ 3 as well as τ 4 , but the second and third preemption of task τ 1 only effect task τ 2 . This is the main idea behind the new algorithm: Several indirect preemptions affect lower priority tasks only once.

Suppose that the first preemption of τ 1 removes some cache blocks of τ 3 . The second activation of τ 1 will remove exactly the same cache blocks, because τ 3 is still stalling. This assumes that all activations of τ 1 would take the same execution path, or equivalently the preemption delay analysis takes all used cache blocks of τ 1 (on any path) into consideration, as described in Sec. 3.1.

For the example we determine the preemption delays that are caused by τ 1 for all lower priority tasks, starting with τ 4 . Task τ 4 is preempted four times (n = 4) by τ 1 . Task τ j could potentially preempt τ k E j (R k ) times for every activation of τ k during the interval R i . If we show that for each activation of τ k the number of preemptions increases by at most one (n p+1 = n p + 1) then Equation 12is shown. Three cases have to be analyzed:

Case 1: Task τ k executes and finishes before the first preemption by τ j occurs. All preemptions impose costs on lower priority tasks and no additional preemption costs have to be considered. The upper bound n p+1 = n p + 1 is safe.

Case 2: Task τ k executes only as long as one and only one preemption by τ j occurs. Hence the number of preemptions has to be incremented by one: n p+1 = n p + 1. All further preemptions by τ j affect lower priority tasks and, consequently, have already been considered in n p .

Case 3: Task τ k executes for a certain time such that τ j preempts τ k l-times, where 2 ≤ l ≤ E j (R k ). For the first preemption the total number of preemptions increases by one, as in case 2. Hence n p+1 = n p + 1. For all remaining l -1 preemptions the total number of preemptions is increased by l -1. But at the same time, l -1 preemptions do not affect any of the lower priority tasks because we have already assumed one preemption by τ j for every lower priority task, that is suspended by τ k . All l -1 further preemptions by τ j do not change the cache contents because the preempting task uses the same cache blocks as during its first execution and cannot replace any additional cache blocks. This is true for direct-mapped caches as well as for set-associative caches, here only the order of cache blocks in the cache set may change. Note that the preemption delay δ j,i has to consider the union of all used cache blocks of the preempting task. A state-wise cache analysis, as described in [12], does not fulfill this assumption. To conclude, for each masked preemption the number of preemptions decreases by one. This results in n p+1 = n p + 1 + (l -1) -(l -1) = n p + 1. As in case 2, none of the remaining E j (R k )l preemptions hit τ k but lower priority tasks which have been considered in n p according to the induction assumption.

We have shown that for each activation of τ k the maximum number of preemptions increases by at most one. Hence we have shown that n p increases at most by n p+1 = n p + E k (R i ) for all E k (R i ) activations during R i . At the end of each iteration ∆ j,i (R i ) extracts the n p+1 largest preemption costs from the set M p+1 . When the iterative algorithm finishes with k = j + 1 then ∆ j,i (R i ) denotes the preemption costs for all possible preemptions that τ j imposes on τ j+1 , •••, τ i . This proves Equation 12.

div.head: Experiments
div.p: The CRPD analysis presented in this paper is compared to the approaches of Petters [14] and Busquets-Mataix et al. [3]. A comparison to more sophisticated scheduling analysis of Lee et al., would have required to re-implement their complex ILP formulation.

In this experiment, the influence of the cache usage, of the preemption costs and of the task periods are compared to the previous approaches. The worst case execution time of each task was determined by a cycle accurate ARM945 processor simulator [1] for different instruction cache architectures with a 20 cycles cache miss penalty. We assumed a direct mapped instruction cache with a cache block size of 8 Byte and a fixed instruction length of 32-bit such that two instructions fit in each cache block. Even though these benchmarks are small, the cache effects due to preemptions can be precisely studied by choosing a suitable cache size. The effects of larger caches used in the embedded controllers will be similar because the CRPD depends on the number of cache blocks that are used by several tasks and not on the cache size alone. Therefore, a cache footprint of all tasks is presented in Figure 4. For several cache sizes the number of cache sets that are potentially used by i tasks is given in percentage (%). This table can be interpreted as a frequency distribution of used cache blocks. For example, for the 1KB cache 41% of all cache sets are potentially used by 2 tasks, 49% are potentially used by 3 tasks and 10% are potentially used by 4 tasks. On average 2.69 tasks use each cache set. To compute this frequency distribution, the maximum number of used cache blocks for each task is computed by data flow analysis [16] and summed up in a usage vector U. For example, the usage distribution for 1024 Byte cache is U = (0, 0, 52, 63, 13, 0), where U[i] denotes the number of cache sets that are potentially used by i tasks. The frequency distribution is calculated by dividing U[i] by the number of cache sets S (U[3]/128 = 63/128 = 0.49). The average us-U avg is computed by
div.formula: U avg = ∑ n i=0 i•U[i] S
div.p: , where n denotes the number of tasks ((52 • 2 + 63 • 3 + 13 • 4)/128 = 2.69). Figure 5 shows the number of used and useful cache blocks for each task which has been calculated by data flow analysis. The first column shows the task id, the second to the 6th columns the number of used cache blocks and the 7th to the 11th columns the useful cache blocks for different cache sizes. These costs are used for the calculation for Busquets-Mataix and Petters approach, respectively. Some of the CRPD costs δ j,i that task τ j imposes on τ i are shown in Figure 6 for task set τ 5 , τ 4 , τ 3 , τ 1 τ 2 (with τ 5 the highest and τ 1 the lowest priority). For example for a 2048 Byte cache, the preemption cost δ 5,3 by τ 5 on τ 3 is bounded in Petters approach by 78 CBs, in Busquets-Mataix by 161 CBs and in our approach by 51 CBs, which is a 34% and 68% improvement, respectively.

The upper diagram in Figure 7 shows the CRPD for a 1KB cache for two task sets calculated by Busquets-Mataix, Petters, the simplified model (Eq. 6) (Sums) and masking algorithm according to Section 3.3 (Sets). The results are normalized with respect to Busquets-Mataix' approach. The new approach gives an average improvement of 70% compared to Busquets-Mataix and about 90% compared to Petters. The lower diagram in Figure 7 is over thousand times greater than the cache miss penalty.

Diagram 8 shows the effect of distinguishing between the npreemption cost. This detailed modeling only shows small improvements (about 15%), because the benchmarks consist of many loops that are iterated several hundred times, such that the most expensive preemptions take place inside a loop body. For linear benchmarks there are is most one cache block useful if an empty cache is assumed. However we have shown in [16] that multiple task activation can profit from cache blocks of previous activations. Figure 9 show the CRPD for different cache usages and task priorities as described in Table 4. For larger caches the improvement of the proposed approach increases up to 90% compared to previous polynomial algorithms. The performance of the analysis was tested with 5, 10 and 25 tasks. The running time of the scheduling analysis was 156, 179 and 454 ms, respectively. This shows that our approach computes the response time for even large task sets in a short time.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper we have proposed a novel polynomial algorithm to determine the cache related preemption delay for fixed priority periodic preemptive scheduling for instruction caches. It includes all cache effects that current polynomial approaches [14] [3] consider with a significantly improved analysis precision. Further more, some effects that are covered in exponentially complex algorithms [10] are analyzed, if the analysis has a polynomial time complexity. Where this is not possible, such considering task phasing, Lee et al. do not deliver an exact solution, as BCETs are needed and multiple preemption costs are approximated by the most expensive preemption costs, which is an overestimation [16].

In the experiments, the influence on the analysis precision of the cache size and different task sets of typical embedded benchmarks was analyzed. The results show significant improvements over previous polynomial approaches.
